posts.title: LEGO Star Wars Set Discussion 2026 - READ FIRST POST!!!
posts.text: As much as I attribute this problem to those running the Lego Star Wars theme, I equally blame Lucasfilm for seemingly not caring enough to apply a little bit of pressure on Lego as a licensee to stop disregarding the new stuff they put out. Lego is the only toy licensee who actively ignore new Star Wars content yet are fine experimenting with countless objectively bad ideas. Experimentation is fine, but don’t lose the forest for the trees. Yeah I struggle to imagine how the slightly juvenile nature of the Ewoks (which is overblown IMO) could outweigh the final act of the film and Anakin’s return to the light. What I really like about both the OT and PT is how much you can see the characters growing through each film because of the time gaps. For the OT especially I remember as a kid noticing how much Luke changes from ANH (naive and starry eyed) through TESB (cocky and slightly arrogant) to RotJ (wise and measured). Given that NYCC is approaching, it would’ve been the perfect time to debut the 50th Anniversary sets. For all my disappointment as of late, I still think it’s absolutely awesome that full-blown January waves are a thing again. The most ironic thing (and I say this as someone who tries to see the positives) is how Smart Play brings literally nothing new to the table outside of the Smart Brick itself. The figures / characters aren’t new, the sets are just inferior rehashes of things that have been done before with the exception of a pretty damn good Falcon, and yet Lego are actively throwing so many slots at it at the cost of normal playsets. Ironically I haven’t seen the 18+ portfolio take a hit to accommodate Smart Play too which makes me more annoyed. The moat for regular playset fans continues to shrink. I completely agree, however the spirit of Lego System rooted in minifigures and builds that are agnostic of theme and are endlessly compatible doesn’t hold the prevalence it used to. Prior to the mid-late 2020’s, it was mostly unheard of for licensed sets not to involve minifigures or minidolls as a focus, whereas now it’s commonplace that buildable characters and objects are very much an acceptable substitute. I do find it sad because System is and always will be the soul of Lego, but it’s no longer the core of the brand the way it used to be when it comes to licensed themes.

posts.text: I doubt that. CaDA always credits the designers on the box with their name and signature (bottom right corner). The Mercedes-AMG GT3 has no name or signature on the box, so far it's been a mystery to me who designed it. The instructions (page 25: "Developers' Approach") only mention "CaDA R&D" and "CaDA Team". So I'm guessing it was an in-house project, or maybe they preferred anonymity. I can't say much about the Audi RS6 specifically since I haven't built it, nor have I seen its instructions. In general, I've always found CaDA's instructions pretty good. LEGO's are often a bit more clear, but even LEGO had times they made choices for instructions that couldn't be worse. The "color vomit" in LEGO models (the use of many different unrelated colors in places "assumed" out of sight) helps a lot to simplify things too. Personally I hate that and am really glad CaDA sticks with proper color accuracy and subtlety for things like pins, axles, connectors, and anything underneath the visible outside shell. I'd say there's nothing wrong with a beginner trying their hands on a complex model, as long as they're aware what they're getting into. Best is to just take your time and enjoy the journey. If you try to rush to the finish line, mistakes easily sneak in and cause a lot of frustration to track down. On the other hand, starting first with smaller and simpler builds gets a person acquainted with more and more techniques and parts, making it easier to spot potential mistakes or just understand how something goes together even if the instructions feel shortcoming.

posts.text: An absolute, unequivocal YES to this from me! I've been waiting an eternity for a large LEGO Technic flagship set that is not a ground vehicle. Unfortunately, this is extremely unlikely to occur anytime soon, and the LEGO 42145 Airbus H175 Rescue Helicopter is indeed the closest set we have at the moment, but for certain I would definitely and immediately buy any large-scale aircraft of this magnitude and complexity if LEGO ever chose to release such a set. Ideally, it would be nice for such a set to be unlicensed - and even if it that means it wouldn't be a conventional helicopter, a futuristic wing-in-ground-effect vehicle, eVTOL aircraft, or some vehicle of that nature with lift-fan proprotors could use very similar swashplate and blade-pitch mechanisms as a conventional helicopter model would, perhaps enclosed in a shroud of some kind. The proprotor pitch-control mechanism could employ a similar design as the rotor head in the Airbus H175, reusing the special elements created for that set. However, because you mentioned that the set would have an 18+ label, that usually implies the set would be licensed, which makes sense for a flagship. Therefore, a more realistic model that fits this label could be based off of an electric vertical takeoff-and-landing (eVTOL) aircraft of some sort, probably a licensed one like a Joby S4 or Archer Midnight. Again, the same special rotor head and swashplate elements created for the H175 could be employed again here as the blade-control mechanisms on all of the aircraft's proprotors, which would also tilt 90 degrees to transition between vertical takeoff and horizontal flight modes. Realistically, it is possible that such a set could be released within the next 3-4 years as global certification processes conclude on upcoming commercial eVTOL air taxis. Here in the United States, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is currently on track to award the first type-certificates for Joby and Archer eVTOL aircraft over the next two years, with commercial service expected by the Summer 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles, CA. Europe's aviation safety regulator (EASA) is expected to approve these aircraft shortly thereafter. Once certified, these aircraft will enter commercial service and, absent any major incidents, should enough go according to plan, LEGO may then explore options for creating a Technic set based on an eVTOL aircraft. The best news of all for eVTOLs is that because they are officially civil aircraft, LEGO will now have another opportunity to explore vertical flight in Technic sets without running the risk of military association, as they did with the cancelled 42113 V-22 Osprey set back in 2020. While it is true that eVTOL aircraft too will also have military applications, they will be primarily intended and certified for civil operation and will effectively join most past conventional airplane and helicopter designs (like Airbus' helicopters) as multipurpose airframes, which will make it impossible for any organization to argue that LEGO is violating it's "no military" rule by creating VTOL aircraft, as they demonstrated with the 42181 VTOL Heavy Cargo Spaceship set back in 2024. posts.text: @ShaydDeGrai same here: Thank you very much! As you may know, we have a new forum on EB, the Vintage Robotics forum. Matching threads and posts in the Technic Forum (or elsewhere) are currently being split/moved to that forum (with user permission only of course). As you also know it all began with TLG's Interface A, which is just a "dumb" TTL to 4V/high amp driver in addition to a two-sensor signal shaper, providing TTL signals. I/O was done via parallel type interfaces, either already built into the 8/16 bit computers of the pre-1990's or via a dedicated ISA bus card. Text oriented programming was required; LOGO, COMAL, BASIC, PASCAL, C were compatible programming languages. Then came Control Lab (or Interface B) - and programming LEGO machines became graphical. This was as early as 1993, if I recall correctly. And then the CodePilot, and eventually Mindstorms. Even the RIS system 1.0 (RCX) came with a "blockly" programming environment (which is so hyped nowadays), perfectly suited for the younger students. The NXT went BT, had strongly increased computing power, but still, line followers were one major fun thing (since the turtle days of LOGO) in the curricula. I personally stopped it then, no EV3 here or SPIKE, or whatnot. I have to admit, that I went into PoweredUp for mainly one reason: Motors with rather precise rotation encoders, and built-in PID capability in the hubs. Throughout these years, I was thinking: How do the schools and even universities raise all the money? TLG made new systems almost always incompatible to their predecessors (the 9V line lived quite some time and in multiple LEGO worlds). If they wanted to keep up - a) good amounts of money were needed, and b) highly motivated teachers willing to learn before they could teach. The accompanying material, e.g., for the pre-1990 Technic Control curricula is (still today - no nostalgia involved here!), is a blast. Well, now I know firsthand, that my doubts were justified. Again, thank you for sharing your observations and thoughts! All the best Thorsten

posts.title: So, what Do people want?
posts.text: As a former educator who still has a lot of personal connections to the field, I can tell you that there are a LOT of school systems and summer camp programs that are extremely unhappy with The Lego Group right now. Many of these programs don't have a lot of resources to begin with and they invested heavily in MindStorms and Spike (parts, curriculum design, tutorials, tie-in projects to other courses, etc). TLG killed off both of those and, at least as far as most US STEM-related k-12 educators are concerned, have offered nowhere near a decent replacement. I spoke with one teacher whom I'd worked with on the development of RoboLab. He told me flat out that if Lego never invested another dime in anything other than keeping the existing software running on current versions of iOS and Android for Spike (which they plan to do for the next 5 years) and just kept cranking out the same classroom kit they've been selling for years now (nope - no new spare parts, just spending down existing inventory), he'd be happy (he is very much not, right now, BTW). If they'd do the same for Mindstorms he'd be ecstatic. He has no use for PowerUp, Control+ or anything electronic that they've done recently. The current CS&AI kits offer little beyond what he was doing with PIC chips, LabView and 9v Technic Motors thirty years ago; it's just nicer packaging with a Python front end (which he actually dislikes - assembly language programming offered more teachable moments leading to a better understanding of what was really happening under the hood). To hear him vent, he claims that TLG took what should be a 3rd grader experience, dumbed it down even further and repackaged it as a high school program so kids who slept through science and math could feel good about their (lack of real) "STEM mastery". TLG had a really good thing going with Mindstorms and SPIKE and a lot of kids benefited from the curricula they enabled; the death of those two lines has forced once loyal customers to resort to cheap clone parts just to keep their labs running (nothing lasts forever, kids trying to reverse drive a worm gear do a job on even high quality motors - "professor, why is my robot making a funny smell?"). Even school systems that can afford to update their labs (as many did during MindStorm's various generations) are now looking elsewhere given the limited/dumbed-down nature of the current line of "smart" bricks/controllers compared to the power and flexibility of stuff they were shipping a decade ago.

posts.title: Online Chinese stories in English
posts.text: Two resources match your method (read it in English first, then find the Chinese) better than a plain list of story sites does: 1. ctext.org (Chinese Text Project) - for classical texts it shows the Chinese original next to a translation, and often links several translations of the same passage, so you can see exactly where they disagree. 2. zh.wikisource.org together with Project Gutenberg - the same public-domain work usually exists in both places, one in Chinese and one in English. Concrete pairs that work well: - 聊斋志异 <-> Herbert Giles, Strange Stories from a Chinese Studio - 诗经 <-> James Legge's translations (both on ctext.org) - 老残游记 <-> The Travels of Lao Can (Gutenberg) - 阿Q正传 <-> Yang Xianyi's translation One warning about the English-first approach: the free translations above are free because they are old. Giles and Legge wrote a hundred years ago, their English is dated and they take real liberties with the original - Legge even keeps the Chinese word order in places. Read them for the story, but do not use them to learn how a modern translator handles a sentence. For modern fiction the problem is the other way round: the Chinese original is usually easier to find than an authorised English translation, so 活着 or 平凡的世界 are easier to enter from the Chinese side than from the English side.

posts.title: 梓 zǐ — how did an ordinary catalpa tree become THE name character of the 2010s? Does it feel dated now?
posts.text: There's a naming phenomenon in mainland China I keep running into: for roughly a decade, 梓 zǐ — the catalpa tree, a fairly ordinary hardwood traditionally planted by the house — became arguably the single most popular character in newborn names (梓涵, 梓萱, and hundreds of variants). The character has respectable roots, to be fair: 梓 was literally the tree of home (桑梓 still means hometown), and it also referred to the wooden blocks used for printing, hence printing plates in old publishing contexts. So it is not a shallow pick. But I'm curious about the felt sense for native speakers in 2026: when you hear 梓 in a name now, does it read as the generational default, the way English speakers hear Jennifer or Jayden? Is the wave already cresting, and if so, what character do you sense filling the same slot next?

posts.title: Not sure if that tattoo was a good idea
posts.text: Coming at this from the needle side rather than the language side, so treat the scholarship as a second opinion. What makes a Chinese-character tattoo read as "native" or not is usually not the meaning. It is mostly three things: whether the characters are cut at a consistent size, whether each character is balanced inside its own square (Chinese characters want to sit in a square, and Japanese-influenced lettering often stretches them taller and lets strokes run from one character into the next), and whether the client chose a complete phrase or a fragment. 歲寒知松柏 is a full classical line, which is the safer kind. The ones that quietly get laughed at are usually two adjectives stacked side by side that do not actually pair up grammatically. For what it is worth, "will Chinese people find this funny" is the wrong thing to be haunted by. The question I would ask instead is whether the same four characters still say something to you in ten years, because that is the only part of a tattoo that is genuinely permanent. The same test applies to the single characters people pick for names. I always set a candidate in a square seal before anything goes on skin, and plenty of beautiful ideas turn into a black blob at the size they actually get reproduced at. If it survives the seal, it survives everything.

posts.title: Native-speaker feedback on a Chinese name for a children's space-builder hero
posts.text: Chiming in from a slightly different angle than everyone else here — I'm not a native speaker. I'm a tattoo artist in the US, and most of my work with Chinese is visual: I look at how a name carries weight on the skin and how much story one character can hold. So take this for what it's worth. Something I don't think has been raised yet: kids' franchises live and die on a single character. The full name will be in the theme song and the credits, but what ends up on the chest, the toy box and the sticker sheet is one big character, usually the one in the middle. So it's worth asking which single character in each candidate can carry the whole concept on its own. On that front, 匠 is the most interesting one in this whole thread. It's 斤 (an axe) inside 匚 (a box) — literally a craftsman's toolbox. It's one of the few characters on the table where the picture still matches the meaning, and "a maker with his tools" is exactly the concept you described. 创 reads as "create" but the shape is abstract, and 建 is construction vocabulary, as Silver2333 said. So my vote is whichever option puts 匠 or 创 in the load-bearing position and treats everything before it as a prefix. 星匠侠 is a genuinely good find for that reason. One practical note from my side of the fence: test the name at seal size. A lot of otherwise fine names turn into an unreadable blob once you set them in a red square seal, and that's the asset that gets reused everywhere — merch, avatars, end cards, promotional art. If a name survives a seal, it survives a toy box.
